items.prompt_en: Read: 'Every Sunday, Nani asked Arjun to read the bus numbers aloud before she left for the market. One morning she said quietly, "I am tired of asking strangers which bus goes where." That evening Arjun drew big letters on an old calendar. Nani traced them with a finger that had shelled peas for sixty years. Some nights she pushed the book away. But a month later, at the bus stop, she read "42 City Market" before Arjun could open his mouth, and laughed like a schoolgirl.' What did Nani ask Arjun to read aloud every Sunday?
items.prompt_hi: Passage dhyaan se padho. Har Sunday Nani Arjun se kya padhwati thi?
items.answer: The bus numbers
hints: Look at the first sentence.
It is something at the bus stop.
Nani asked Arjun to read the bus ___.
She asked him to read the bus numbers.

items.prompt_en: Read: 'Every Sunday, Nani asked Arjun to read the bus numbers aloud before she left for the market. Nani traced them with a finger that had shelled peas for sixty years. Some nights she pushed the book away. But a month later, at the bus stop, she read "42 City Market" before Arjun could open his mouth, and laughed like a schoolgirl.' Why did Nani want to learn to read? Give the clue from the passage.
items.prompt_hi: Nani padhna kyun seekhna chahti thi? Passage ki woh line batao jo isse prove kare.
items.answer: She was tired of asking strangers which bus to take; she wanted to manage on her own
acceptable: she did not want to depend on strangers
she was tired of asking others
to read the bus numbers herself
hints: What did she say one morning?
Who did she have to ask every time?
She said she was tired of asking ___.
She wanted to be independent instead of asking strangers.

items.prompt_en: Read: 'Every Sunday, Nani asked Arjun to read the bus numbers aloud before she left for the market. Nani traced them with a finger that had shelled peas for sixty years. Some nights she pushed the book away. items.prompt_hi: 'laughed like a schoolgirl' — is line se Nani ke feelings ke baare mein kya pata chalta hai?
items.answer: She felt joyful, proud and young again, because she had finally learnt something new, like a child at school
hints: Who usually laughs like a schoolgirl?
What had she just done?
She felt ___ because she read the number herself.
She felt proud and young again, like a child who has just learnt something.

items.prompt_en: Read: 'Every Sunday, Nani asked Arjun to read the bus numbers aloud before she left for the market. One morning she said quietly, "I am tired of asking strangers which bus goes where." That evening Arjun drew big letters on an old calendar. Nani traced them with a finger that had shelled peas for sixty years. Some nights she pushed the book away. items.prompt_hi: Aage kya hoga? Agle Sunday Nani kya karegi?
items.answer: She will read the bus number herself and go to the market without asking anyone
acceptable: read the bus numbers by herself
she will not need Arjun's help
hints: What can she do now that she could not do before?
Will she still need to ask strangers?
Next Sunday she will read the bus number ___.
She will read it herself and go alone.

items.answer: B is the theme; A is a plot summary
acceptable: A is summary, B is theme
hints: Which one has names in it?
Which one is true for anyone, not just Nani?
The theme is the sentence without ___.
B is the theme because it is a general idea; A only retells the events.

items.prompt_en: Your younger cousin read a story where a girl teaches her grandmother to read. Explain to her, in three or four sentences, what such a story is really about beyond what happens.
items.prompt_hi: Socho tum apni chhoti cousin ko samjha rahe ho. Kahani mein kya hua, woh nahi — kahani asal mein kis baare mein hai, yeh batao.
items.answer: Learning has no age limit; a young person can teach an elder; reading gives independence and self-respect; both need patience and love
acceptable: it is never too late to learn
young people can teach old people
the bond between grandparent and grandchild
hints: What did the grandmother gain besides letters?
Who taught whom, and why is that unusual?
The story shows that learning has no ___.
Key idea: learning has no age, it brings independence, and it grows a bond between generations.

items.prompt_en: Join the two ideas using 'had': 'Nani shelled peas for sixty years. Then she learnt to read.' Begin with: 'Before she learnt to read, Nani ...'
items.prompt_hi: Do sentences ko jodo. Jo kaam pehle hua, uske saath 'had' lagega.
items.answer: Before she learnt to read, Nani had shelled peas for sixty years.
acceptable: Before she learned to read, Nani had shelled peas for sixty years.
Before she learnt to read, Nani had shelled peas for 60 years.
hints: Which action happened first?
The earlier action gets had + V3.
Before she learnt to read, Nani ___ shelled peas for sixty years.
Before she learnt to read, Nani had shelled peas for sixty years.

items.prompt_en: Find and correct the mistake: 'When Arjun reached the bus stop, the bus already left, so they waited for the next one.'
items.prompt_hi: Is sentence mein ek galti hai. Bus pehle gayi ya Arjun pehle pahuncha? Socho.
items.answer: When Arjun reached the bus stop, the bus had already left, so they waited for the next one.
hints: Which happened first: reaching or leaving?
The earlier past action needs a helper.
the bus ___ already left
Correct: 'the bus had already left', because it left before Arjun reached.

items.prompt_en: One word in this sentence is not needed. Find it and say why: 'Last year my grandmother had joined an adult literacy class.'
items.prompt_hi: Ek word extra hai. Yahaan koi doosra past event hai kya jiske pehle yeh hua?
items.answer: Remove 'had': 'Last year my grandmother joined an adult literacy class.' There is only one past event, so past simple is enough
acceptable: Last year my grandmother joined an adult literacy class.
hints: How many past events are in the sentence?
'had + V3' needs another past event to compare with.
Last year my grandmother ___ an adult literacy class.
Use 'joined'; past perfect is only for the earlier of two past events.

items.prompt_en: Say the opposite of each word with the correct prefix: literate, patient, possible, regular.
items.prompt_hi: Har word ka ulta banao. Pehla letter dekho — il-, im-, ir- ya un-?
items.answer: illiterate, impatient, impossible, irregular
hints: Look at the first letter of each word.
Before l use il-, before p use im-, before r use ir-.
lit- becomes il-literate, pat- becomes im-___.
illiterate, impatient, impossible, irregular.

items.prompt_en: Fill the blank with a word from the 'literate' family: 'The village started a ___ drive so that every adult could learn to read.'
items.prompt_hi: 'literate' parivaar ka kaunsa word yahaan fit hoga? Yeh noun chahiye.
items.answer: literacy
hints: Is the blank a person, a quality or an action?
It names the idea of being able to read.
liter-___
literacy: a literacy drive.

items.prompt_en: Your friend says in Hindi: 'Seekhne ki koi umar nahi hoti.' Say this idea in natural English as the first sentence (the claim) of a paragraph about the story.
items.prompt_hi: Is Hindi baat ko natural English mein bolo — word-by-word nahi, jaise ek angrez bolega.
items.answer: There is no age limit for learning.
acceptable: It is never too late to learn.
One is never too old to learn.
You are never too old to learn.
hints: Don't translate word by word.
Think of 'never too ___ to learn'.
It is never too ___ to learn.
Natural English: 'It is never too late to learn.'

items.prompt_en: Write three sentences on 'Arjun was a good teacher': one claim, one piece of evidence from the passage, one explanation.
items.prompt_hi: Teen sentence: pehle apni baat (claim), phir passage se saboot (evidence), phir samjhao kyun (explanation).
items.answer: Claim: Arjun was a patient, thoughtful teacher. Evidence: he drew big letters on an old calendar and kept going even when Nani pushed the book away. Explanation: he fitted the lesson to her needs and gave her time, so she succeeded in a month
acceptable: he was patient because he did not give up when she pushed the book away
he drew big letters on a calendar to make it easy
claim, evidence, explanation about his patience and creativity
hints: What did Arjun actually do in the passage?
Pick one action that shows a good teacher.
Claim: Arjun was ___. Evidence: he ___. This shows ___.
A full answer names a quality, quotes an action like the calendar letters, and explains why it helped.

workedExample.problem: Combine with 'after' and 'had': 'Nani learnt the alphabet. Then she read the bus number.'
steps: Find which action happened first: learning the alphabet.
Give the earlier action 'had + past participle': 'had learnt'.
Keep the later action in past simple: 'read'.
Join with 'after' before the earlier action.
Answer: After Nani had learnt the alphabet, she read the bus number.

Labels every figurative line 'simile'

Yes, because it compares rivers to gold

items.prompt_en: Read this poem: 'From snow that crowns the northern hills / to waves that wash the southern sand, / a hundred tongues, one heartbeat fills / the mother-soil we call our land. // Her rivers braid the plains with gold, / her deserts keep the stars at night; / her stories, new and centuries old, / are woven threads of shade and light.' Which two places, at opposite ends of the land, does the first stanza mention?
items.prompt_hi: Pehle stanza mein desh ke do kone kaunse hain? Ek north, ek south.
items.answer: The snowy northern hills and the southern sand (seashore)
acceptable: snowy mountains and the southern beach
the north hills and the south sea
hints: Look at lines one and two.
One is cold, one is by the sea.
From snow on the northern ___ to the southern ___.
The snowy northern hills and the southern sand.

items.prompt_en: Read this poem: 'From snow that crowns the northern hills / to waves that wash the southern sand, / a hundred tongues, one heartbeat fills / the mother-soil we call our land. // Her rivers braid the plains with gold, / her deserts keep the stars at night; / her stories, new and centuries old, / are woven threads of shade and light.' The poet calls the land 'mother-soil'. Why?
items.prompt_hi: Desh ko 'mother-soil' kyun kaha? Maa se kya rishta hota hai?
items.answer: Because the land feeds, shelters and holds everyone together like a mother; it shows love and reverence
acceptable: the land is like a mother who cares for us
it shows love and respect for the land
the land nourishes us like a mother
hints: What does a mother do for her children?
Does the land do something similar?
The land ___ us like a mother.
The land nourishes and unites us like a mother, so the poet speaks of it with love and respect.

items.prompt_en: Name the device: 'Her deserts keep the stars at night.'
items.prompt_hi: Desert koi insaan hai kya? Phir bhi woh 'keep' kar raha hai. Yeh kaunsa device hai?
items.answer: Personification
hints: Can a desert really keep something?
Who usually keeps or guards things?
A non-human thing doing a human action is ___.
Personification: the desert is given the human action of keeping.

items.prompt_en: Compare: A: 'The river is like a golden ribbon.' B: 'Her rivers braid the plains with gold.' Which is a simile, which is personification, and which feels stronger to you?
items.prompt_hi: Dono lines dhyaan se suno. Ek mein 'like' hai, ek mein nahi. Farak batao.
items.answer: A is a simile (it uses 'like'); B is personification (rivers braid like hands). B is more direct and vivid because the rivers are shown acting
acceptable: A is simile, B is metaphor or personification
hints: Which one has 'like'?
In B, what action do the rivers do?
A uses ___ so it is a simile; B gives rivers a ___ action.
A is a simile; B is personification, which shows the rivers working like hands and feels more vivid.

items.prompt_en: Look at the end words of the first stanza: hills, sand, fills, land. Write the rhyme scheme.
items.prompt_hi: Last words ki awaaz milao. Jo same awaaz, usko same letter do.
items.answer: ABAB
hints: Does 'hills' rhyme with 'fills'?
Does 'sand' rhyme with 'land'?
hills = A, sand = B, fills = ___, land = ___.
ABAB.

items.prompt_hi: Is student ne galat device bataya. Sahi kya hai aur kyun?
items.answer: It is not a simile because there is no 'like' or 'as'; it is personification (the rivers braid, a human action)
acceptable: it is a metaphor, not a simile
hints: Is there a 'like' or 'as' in the line?
What are the rivers doing?
It is not a simile; it is ___.
Correct: it is personification, since the rivers are given the human action of braiding.

Explain 'a hundred tongues, one heartbeat' in plain English. You can also give the Hindi phrase that matches it.

items.answer: Many languages, but one shared feeling: unity in diversity (anekta mein ekta)
hints: What can 'tongue' mean besides a body part?
Think of 'mother tongue'.
Many ___, but one shared ___.
It means many languages but one shared heart: unity in diversity.

What is the tone of the poem? Name two words that show it.
items.prompt_hi: Poet kis bhaav se bol raha hai? Do words dhoondho jo yeh dikhaate hain.
items.answer: Proud and loving (reverent); words such as 'crowns', 'mother-soil', 'gold', 'heartbeat'

Which words sound royal or precious?

diversity, unity, pride, freedom.

acceptable: Our class shows diversity in food and festivals.
There is a lot of diversity in my colony.

items.prompt_en: Why might a poet writing about a whole country choose a regular rhyme and steady beat?

items.answer: A steady rhythm sounds like a song or anthem, gives a feeling of harmony and togetherness, and is easy to remember and recite together

How does a steady beat feel?
A regular beat makes the poem sound like an ___.
It sounds like an anthem, suggesting harmony, and it is easy to recite together.

items.prompt_en: Read: 'Anjali failed her first state-level swimming trial by four seconds. She cried in the bus all the way home. The next morning her coach was at the pool at five. "If you train like this every day for a year," he said, "you will cut those four seconds." She did not give up. Some mornings the water was so cold that her hands went numb; some evenings she wanted to quit. She kept a notebook and wrote down her time after every practice, even on bad days. A year later, she qualified by half a second. "The medal was nice," she says now, "but the notebook is what I keep."' By how many seconds did Anjali fail her first trial?
items.prompt_hi: Anjali pehle trial mein kitne seconds se reh gayi?
items.answer: Four seconds
hints: Look at the first sentence.
It is a small number.
She failed by ___ seconds.
Four seconds.

acceptable: failure is a step, not the end
practise daily and track your progress
Anjali failed too but kept going
hints: What happened to Anjali first?
How did she change the result?
Failing once doesn't mean ___; steady practice can ___.
Key idea: setbacks are normal; steady, tracked practice turns failure into success.

items.prompt_en: Write a four-sentence paragraph about a time you, or someone you know, kept trying after a setback: a topic sentence, two details and a closing line.
items.prompt_hi: Ek paragraph likho: kisi ne haar ke baad bhi koshish jaari rakhi. Topic sentence, do details, aur ek closing line.
items.answer: A topic sentence naming the person and setback, two specific details of continued effort, and a closing line on the lesson, e.g. 'My cousin failed her driving test the first time. She practised every evening with my uncle. She also watched videos on parking. When she passed a month later, she said the practice mattered more than the licence.'
acceptable: My brother lost the chess final but practised daily and won the next year.
hints: Who faced the setback?
What did they do afterwards, exactly?
Topic: ___ failed ___. Details: ___ and ___. Closing: ___.
A full paragraph has a clear topic sentence, two concrete details and a closing lesson.

skills.title: Identify the speaker's purpose and audience: the imperative mood and 'you' addressing the reader
Explain the metaphors (hill, sky, stumble as a name), the personification of doubt and the rhetorical question
Form imperatives and negative imperatives correctly (Don't give up; Never compare)
Tell self-belief apart from arrogance and use the vocabulary of confidence (confident, self-doubt, determined, humble)

expectations: Says the poem speaks directly to the reader ('you') to encourage them, like a coach or friend
Explains 'every hill takes time': big goals need patient, step-by-step effort
Explains 'don't let one stumble be your name': one failure does not define you
Identifies the rhetorical question and its expected answer: no one can deny the sky to someone who keeps trying
Distinguishes self-belief (trusting you can grow with effort) from arrogance (thinking you are better than others)
